pillars.name: Operational Excellence
pillars.summary: A commitment to build software correctly while consistently delivering a great customer experience: organizing teams, designing workloads, operating them at scale, and evolving them over time. Best-practice areas: Organization, Prepare, Operate, Evolve.

designPrinciples.title: Organize teams around business outcomes
designPrinciples.detail: Leadership vision, a business-aligned cloud operating model and KPIs aligned at every level let teams operate efficiently toward measurable outcomes.

designPrinciples.title: Implement observability for actionable insights
designPrinciples.detail: Understand workload behavior, performance, reliability, cost and health through telemetry and KPIs so you can act quickly when business outcomes are at risk.

designPrinciples.title: Safely automate where possible
designPrinciples.detail: Define the workload and its operations as code and trigger them from events, with guardrails such as rate control, error thresholds and approvals.

designPrinciples.title: Make frequent, small, reversible changes
designPrinciples.detail: Loosely coupled, automatically deployed components let you ship small increments that reduce blast radius and can be rolled back fast.

designPrinciples.title: Refine operations procedures frequently
designPrinciples.detail: Review and validate runbooks regularly, fix gaps, communicate changes, and use game days to keep teams familiar with procedures.

designPrinciples.title: Anticipate failure
designPrinciples.detail: Drive failure scenarios to understand the risk profile, test procedures and team response against simulated failures, and manage the open risks you find.

designPrinciples.title: Learn from all operational events and metrics
designPrinciples.detail: Run post-incident analysis (e.g. correction-of-error reviews) and share learnings across the organization.

designPrinciples.title: Use managed services
designPrinciples.detail: Reduce operational burden by using AWS managed services where possible and build procedures around interactions with them.

keyQuestions: OPS 1. How do you determine what your priorities are?
OPS 3. How does your organizational culture support your business outcomes?
OPS 4. How do you implement observability in your workload?
OPS 5. How do you reduce defects, ease remediation, and improve flow into production?
OPS 6. How do you mitigate deployment risks?
OPS 7. How do you know that you are ready to support a workload?
OPS 10. How do you manage workload and operations events?
OPS 11. How do you evolve operations?
antiPatterns: Manual, console-driven ("ClickOps") changes to production with no infrastructure as code
Large, infrequent "big bang" releases with no automated rollback
Monitoring only infrastructure metrics (CPU) instead of business KPIs and customer experience
Runbooks that exist only in someone's head or are never exercised in game days
No post-incident review, so the same failure recurs
Alert fatigue: paging on every metric without clear ownership or actionability

pillars.name: Security
pillars.summary: The ability to protect data, systems and assets while taking advantage of cloud technologies to improve your security. Best-practice areas: Security foundations, Identity and access management, Detection, Infrastructure protection, Data protection, Incident response, Application security.

designPrinciples.title: Implement a strong identity foundation
designPrinciples.detail: Apply least privilege and separation of duties, centralize identity management, and eliminate reliance on long-term static credentials.

designPrinciples.title: Maintain traceability
designPrinciples.detail: Monitor, alert on and audit actions and changes in real time, and integrate logs and metrics with systems that automatically investigate and act.

designPrinciples.title: Apply security at all layers
designPrinciples.detail: Defense in depth: controls at the edge, VPC, load balancer, every instance and compute service, operating system, application and code.

designPrinciples.title: Automate security best practices
designPrinciples.detail: Define and manage controls as code in version-controlled templates so secure architectures scale quickly and cost-effectively.

designPrinciples.title: Protect data in transit and at rest
designPrinciples.detail: Classify data by sensitivity and apply encryption, tokenization and access control as appropriate.

designPrinciples.title: Keep people away from data
designPrinciples.detail: Use mechanisms and tools that reduce or eliminate direct human access to data, reducing mishandling and human error.

designPrinciples.title: Prepare for security events
designPrinciples.detail: Have incident management and investigation processes, run response simulations, and automate detection, investigation and recovery.

keyQuestions: SEC 1. How do you securely operate your workload?
SEC 2. How do you manage authentication for people and machines?
SEC 3. How do you manage permissions for people and machines?
SEC 4. How do you detect and investigate security events?
SEC 5. How do you protect your network resources?
SEC 7. How do you classify your data?
SEC 8. How do you protect your data at rest?
SEC 10. How do you anticipate, respond to, and recover from incidents?
SEC 11. How do you incorporate and validate the security properties of applications throughout the design, development, and deployment lifecycle?
antiPatterns: Long-lived IAM user access keys embedded in code or CI systems
Using the root user for daily operations or leaving it without MFA
Wildcard IAM policies ("Action": "*", "Resource": "*") instead of least privilege
All workloads in a single AWS account with no SCP guardrails
Security groups open to 0.0.0.0/0 on management ports
Encryption treated as optional, or no data classification
No incident response playbooks or never simulating an incident
pillars.diagram:
flowchart TD u[Internet]:::user shield@svc(shield, "Edge: Shield") waf@svc(waf, "Edge: WAF") cf@svc(cloudfront) subgraph vpc["VPC"] nfw@svc(network-firewall, "Network
inspection") alb@svc(elb, "ALB · public subnet") app@svc(ecs, "App · private subnet
security groups") db@svc(rds, "Data · encrypted") end iam@svc(iam, "Least-privilege
roles") kms@svc(kms, "Keys") gd@svc(guardduty, "Detect") ct@svc(cloudtrail, "Trace") u --> shield --> waf --> cf --> nfw --> alb --> app --> db app -.- iam db -.- kms db ~~~ gd gd ~~~ ct
pillars.diagramCaption: Defense in depth: a control at every layer (edge, network, compute, data, identity), plus detection and traceability across all of them.

pillars.name: Reliability
pillars.summary: The ability of a workload to perform its intended function correctly and consistently when expected. Best-practice areas: Foundations, Workload architecture, Change management, Failure management.

designPrinciples.title: Automatically recover from failure
designPrinciples.detail: Monitor business-value KPIs and trigger automation when thresholds are breached, so failures are notified, tracked and worked around automatically.

designPrinciples.title: Test recovery procedures
designPrinciples.detail: In the cloud you can test how your workload fails and validate recovery by simulating failures or replaying past incidents.

designPrinciples.title: Scale horizontally to increase aggregate workload availability
designPrinciples.detail: Replace one large resource with multiple small ones so no single failure takes the workload down, and ensure they share no common point of failure.

designPrinciples.title: Stop guessing capacity
designPrinciples.detail: Monitor demand and utilization and automate adding or removing resources to avoid saturation, while managing service quotas.

designPrinciples.title: Manage change through automation
designPrinciples.detail: Make infrastructure changes through automation that is itself tracked and reviewed.

keyQuestions: REL 1. How do you manage Service Quotas and constraints?
REL 2. How do you plan your network topology?
REL 4. How do you design interactions in a distributed system to prevent failures?
REL 5. How do you design interactions in a distributed system to mitigate or withstand failures?
REL 7. How do you design your workload to adapt to changes in demand?
REL 9. How do you back up data?
REL 10. How do you use fault isolation to protect your workload?
REL 13. How do you plan for disaster recovery (DR)?
antiPatterns: Single-AZ deployments or a single NAT gateway/instance for the whole VPC
Retries without exponential backoff and jitter, causing retry storms
Synchronous, tightly coupled calls chains with no timeouts or circuit breakers
Backups that are never restore-tested
Failover plans that depend on control-plane operations during a regional event
Ignoring service quotas until they cause an outage during a traffic spike
Overlapping CIDR ranges that block future peering or Transit Gateway connectivity
pillars.diagram:
flowchart TD u[Clients]:::user r53@svc(route53, "Health-checked
DNS") subgraph region["Region"] alb@svc(elb, "ALB health checks") subgraph aza["AZ a"] a1@svc(ec2, "Instance") end subgraph azb["AZ b"] b1@svc(ec2, "Instance") end q@svc(sqs, "Buffer queue") db@svc(aurora, "Multi-AZ DB") end retry[Timeouts + retries
exponential backoff + jitter]:::note bk@svc(aws-backup, "Tested backups") u --> r53 --> alb alb --> a1 alb --> b1 a1 --> db b1 -->|async| q retry -.- a1 db -.-> bk
pillars.diagramCaption: Remove single points of failure (multiple AZs behind health checks), decouple with queues, bound calls with timeouts and jittered retries, and prove recovery with tested backups.

pillars.name: Performance Efficiency
pillars.summary: The ability to use cloud resources efficiently to meet performance requirements and to maintain that efficiency as demand changes and technologies evolve. Best-practice areas: Architecture selection, Compute and hardware, Data management, Networking and content delivery, Process and culture.

designPrinciples.title: Democratize advanced technologies
designPrinciples.detail: Consume complex technologies (NoSQL, media transcoding, ML) as managed services so your team focuses on product, not provisioning.

designPrinciples.title: Go global in minutes
designPrinciples.detail: Deploy to multiple AWS Regions to provide lower latency and a better customer experience at minimal cost.

designPrinciples.title: Use serverless architectures
designPrinciples.detail: Remove the need to run and maintain servers; managed services operate at cloud scale and can lower transactional costs.

designPrinciples.title: Experiment more often
designPrinciples.detail: Virtual, automatable resources make it cheap to run comparative tests of instance types, storage and configurations.

designPrinciples.title: Consider mechanical sympathy
designPrinciples.detail: Use the technology approach that aligns with your workload goals, e.g. choose databases based on data access patterns.

keyQuestions: PERF 1. How do you select appropriate cloud resources and architecture for your workload?
PERF 2. How do you select and use compute resources in your workload?
PERF 3. How do you store, manage, and access data in your workload?
PERF 4. How do you select and configure networking resources in your workload?
PERF 5. How do your organizational practices and culture contribute to performance efficiency in your workload?
antiPatterns: Choosing one database for every access pattern ("everything in a relational DB")
Using the same instance family for years without benchmarking newer generations (e.g. Graviton)
Serving global users from a single Region without a CDN
No load testing before launch; discovering bottlenecks in production
Chatty cross-AZ or cross-Region calls on the hot path

pillars.name: Cost Optimization
pillars.summary: The ability to run systems that deliver business value at the lowest price point. Best-practice areas: Practice Cloud Financial Management, Expenditure and usage awareness, Cost-effective resources, Manage demand and supply resources, Optimize over time.

designPrinciples.title: Implement Cloud Financial Management
designPrinciples.detail: Dedicate people, programs and processes to build FinOps capability, just as you would for security or operations.

designPrinciples.title: Adopt a consumption model
designPrinciples.detail: Pay only for what you use and scale with business need; e.g. stopping dev/test outside working hours can save ~75% (40 vs 168 hours).

designPrinciples.title: Measure overall efficiency
designPrinciples.detail: Measure business output against the cost of delivering it (unit economics) to know the gains from optimization.

designPrinciples.title: Stop spending money on undifferentiated heavy lifting
designPrinciples.detail: Let AWS handle data centers and, via managed services, OS and application management, so you focus on customers.

designPrinciples.title: Analyze and attribute expenditure
designPrinciples.detail: Accurately identify and attribute cost to workload owners (tags, accounts) to measure ROI and drive optimization.

keyQuestions: COST 1. How do you implement cloud financial management?
COST 2. How do you govern usage?
COST 3. How do you monitor your cost and usage?
COST 4. How do you decommission resources?
COST 6. How do you meet cost targets when you select resource type, size and number?
COST 7. How do you use pricing models to reduce cost?
COST 8. How do you plan for data transfer charges?
COST 9. How do you manage demand, and supply resources?
antiPatterns: No tagging strategy or account structure, so cost cannot be attributed
Buying Reserved Instances/Savings Plans before rightsizing
Running dev/test 24x7 at production size
Ignoring data transfer (NAT gateway, cross-AZ, internet egress) in designs
Keeping all data in S3 Standard forever with no lifecycle policy
Treating cost as a one-time cleanup rather than a continuous practice
pillars.diagram:
flowchart TD w{Workload shape?}:::note sp@svc(savings-plans, "Savings Plans") asg@svc(ec2-auto-scaling, "On-Demand +
scaling") spot@svc(ec2, "Spot
up to 90% off") w -->|steady| sp w -->|spiky| asg w -->|interruptible| spot sp ~~~ asg ~~~ spot
pillars.diagramCaption: Match the pricing model to the usage pattern: commit on the steady baseline, scale On-Demand or serverless for peaks, and put interruptible work on Spot.

pillars.name: Sustainability
pillars.summary: Understanding the environmental impact of the services used, quantifying it across the workload lifecycle, and applying design principles to reduce it. Best-practice areas: Region selection, Alignment to demand, Software and architecture, Data, Hardware and services, Process and culture.

designPrinciples.title: Understand your impact
designPrinciples.detail: Measure and model the impact of your workload, including customer use and decommissioning, and track resources per unit of work as KPIs.

designPrinciples.title: Establish sustainability goals
designPrinciples.detail: Set long-term goals per workload (e.g. compute and storage per transaction) and architect so growth reduces impact intensity.

designPrinciples.title: Maximize utilization
designPrinciples.detail: Right-size and minimize idle resources: two hosts at 30% utilization are less efficient than one at 60%.

designPrinciples.title: Anticipate and adopt new, more efficient hardware and software offerings
designPrinciples.detail: Continually evaluate and design for flexibility so you can quickly adopt more efficient options such as newer instance generations.

designPrinciples.title: Use managed services
designPrinciples.detail: Shared managed services (Fargate, S3 Lifecycle, Auto Scaling) maximize utilization across customers and reduce the infrastructure needed.

designPrinciples.title: Reduce the downstream impact of your cloud workloads
designPrinciples.detail: Reduce the energy and resources customers need to use your service, and avoid forcing device upgrades.

keyQuestions: SUS 1. How do you select Regions for your workload?
SUS 2. How do you align cloud resources to your demand?
SUS 3. How do you take advantage of software and architecture patterns to support your sustainability goals?
SUS 4. How do you take advantage of data management policies and patterns to support your sustainability goals?
SUS 5. How do you select and use cloud hardware and services in your architecture to support your sustainability goals?
SUS 6. How do your organizational processes support your sustainability goals?
antiPatterns: Over-provisioned, always-on capacity for spiky or batch workloads
Storing and backing up data that is easy to recreate or never read
Choosing a Region only on habit without considering latency, requirements and carbon intensity
Using x86 or GPU instances where Graviton or purpose-built accelerators would do the job with less energy

drStrategies.name: Backup and restore
drStrategies.rpo: Hours (as frequent as backups/continuous PITR allow)
drStrategies.cost: $ — lowest; pay only for backup storage and cross-Region copies
drStrategies.description: Back up data (and AMIs, code, configuration) and copy it to the DR Region/account; redeploy infrastructure with IaC at recovery time. Also the baseline defence against data corruption and ransomware for every other strategy. Automate and regularly test restores, since restore is a control-plane operation.
drStrategies.diagram:
flowchart TD u[Users]:::user subgraph pri["Primary Region · active"] app1@svc(ec2, "App") db1@svc(rds, "Database") bk1@svc(aws-backup, "Backups") end subgraph dr["DR Region · nothing running"] bk2@svc(aws-backup, "Backup copies") s3@svc(s3, "AMIs, code") iac@svc(cloudformation, "IaC redeploy
on disaster") end u --> app1 --> db1 db1 --> bk1 bk1 -->|cross-Region copy| bk2 iac -.->|restore + deploy| bk2
drStrategies.diagramCaption: Only backups live in the DR Region; on disaster you restore data and redeploy everything with IaC, so RTO/RPO are hours but cost is lowest.

drStrategies.name: Pilot light
drStrategies.cost: $$ — data tier always on, compute switched off
drStrategies.description: Data is continuously replicated to live data stores in the DR Region and core infrastructure is provisioned, but application servers are "switched off" (ideally not deployed) and must be turned on and scaled out on failover. AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery implements this pattern for server-based workloads. Use Route 53 / Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) for data-plane traffic switching.
drStrategies.diagram:
flowchart TD u[Users]:::user r53@svc(route53) subgraph pri["Primary Region · active"] app1@svc(ec2-auto-scaling, "App fleet") db1@svc(aurora, "Primary DB") end subgraph dr["DR Region · data only"] app2[App servers
switched off]:::note db2@svc(aurora, "Replica DB
always on") end u --> r53 -->|all traffic| app1 --> db1 db1 -->|continuous replication| db2 r53 -.->|after failover| app2 app2 -.->|turn on + scale| db2
drStrategies.diagramCaption: Data is continuously replicated and always on in the DR Region, but compute is off; failover means deploying/starting servers, so RTO is tens of minutes.

drStrategies.name: Warm standby
drStrategies.cost: $$$ — scaled-down but fully functional copy running 24x7
drStrategies.description: A scaled-down, fully functional copy of production runs in the DR Region and can serve traffic immediately at reduced capacity; recovery only requires scaling up (ensure DR-Region quotas allow it). Easier to test continuously. Provisioning full capacity makes it a "hot standby".
drStrategies.diagram:
flowchart TD u[Users]:::user r53@svc(route53) subgraph pri["Primary Region · 100%"] alb1@svc(elb, "ALB") app1@svc(ec2-auto-scaling, "Full fleet") db1@svc(aurora, "Primary DB") end subgraph dr["DR Region · scaled down, running"] alb2@svc(elb, "ALB") app2@svc(ec2-auto-scaling, "Small fleet
scale up on failover") db2@svc(aurora, "Replica DB") end u --> r53 r53 -->|active| alb1 --> app1 --> db1 r53 -.->|failover| alb2 --> app2 --> db2 db1 -->|replication| db2
drStrategies.diagramCaption: A smaller but fully working copy runs in the DR Region and can take traffic immediately; recovery is just scaling up, so RTO is minutes.

drStrategies.name: Multi-site active/active
drStrategies.rpo: Near zero; zero with DynamoDB global tables MRSC or Aurora DSQL multi-Region (data corruption still needs backups)
drStrategies.cost: $$$$ — full production capacity in 2+ Regions plus complexity
drStrategies.description: The workload serves traffic from multiple Regions simultaneously, so there is no failover, only traffic being routed away from an impaired Region. Choose a write strategy: write global (Aurora Global Database, promotion in <1 min), write local (DynamoDB global tables, last-writer-wins or multi-Region strong consistency since June 2025), write partitioned, or strongly consistent multi-Region SQL with Aurora DSQL (GA May 2025). Point-in-time backups are still required.
drStrategies.diagram:
flowchart TD
u[Users]:::user
r53@svc(route53, "Latency routing")
subgraph ra["Region A · active"]
  alb1@svc(elb, "ALB")
  app1@svc(ec2-auto-scaling, "Full fleet")
  db1@svc(dynamodb, "Global table")
end
subgraph rb["Region B · active"]
  alb2@svc(elb, "ALB")
  app2@svc(ec2-auto-scaling, "Full fleet")
  db2@svc(dynamodb, "Global table")
end
u --> r53
r53 --> alb1 --> app1 --> db1
r53 --> alb2 --> app2 --> db2
db1 <-->|multi-active replication| db2
drStrategies.diagramCaption: Both Regions serve traffic at full capacity with multi-active data, so losing a Region only means routing users away; RTO near zero, cost highest.

migrationStrategies.name: Retire
migrationStrategies.description: Decommission or archive applications with no business value, e.g. "zombie" apps under 5% CPU/memory utilization or with no inbound connections for 90 days.
migrationStrategies.example: Portfolio discovery finds 40 internal reporting servers with no logins in 90 days; archive their data to S3 Glacier and shut them down instead of migrating.

migrationStrategies.name: Retain
migrationStrategies.description: Keep the application in the source environment for now, due to compliance, high risk, unresolved dependencies, recent upgrades, a pending SaaS replacement, or mainframe/non-x86 platforms needing more assessment.
migrationStrategies.example: An AS/400 manufacturing system tied to plant-floor hardware stays on premises and is reached from AWS over Direct Connect until a modernization plan exists.

migrationStrategies.name: Rehost (lift and shift)
migrationStrategies.description: Move applications to AWS without changes, at scale, with minimal disruption; optimize after migration. Automated with AWS Application Migration Service (AWS Transform MGN), Cloud Migration Factory or VM Import/Export.
migrationStrategies.example: Replicate 300 on-prem Windows and Linux VMs block-level to EC2 using AWS Application Migration Service, then cut over in waves.

migrationStrategies.name: Relocate
migrationStrategies.description: Move many servers at once to a cloud version of the same platform, or move instances/objects to another VPC, Region or account, with no new hardware, rewrites or operational changes.
migrationStrategies.example: Move a VMware vSphere estate to a VMware-based environment on AWS (e.g. Amazon Elastic VMware Service) using HCX, or move an RDS instance into a different account.

migrationStrategies.name: Repurchase (drop and shop)
migrationStrategies.description: Replace the application with a different product, typically SaaS, to cut maintenance, infrastructure and licensing cost.
migrationStrategies.example: Replace a self-hosted CRM with a SaaS CRM, migrate its data, and integrate authentication with the corporate IdP.

migrationStrategies.name: Replatform (lift, tinker and shift)
migrationStrategies.description: Move to the cloud with targeted optimizations such as managed databases, containers, Graviton or Linux, without changing core architecture.
migrationStrategies.example: Move self-managed SQL Server to Amazon RDS for SQL Server, or containerize a Java app with App2Container and run it on ECS Fargate.

migrationStrategies.name: Refactor or re-architect
migrationStrategies.description: Re-architect using cloud-native features to improve agility, performance and scalability. Most complex and costly; AWS recommends modernizing after the migration for large programs.
migrationStrategies.example: Break an on-prem Oracle-backed monolith into microservices on Lambda/ECS with Aurora PostgreSQL and DynamoDB, or refactor COBOL to Java with AWS Transform for mainframe.
